content:
I hate all the talk about gratitude.

Not because gratitude isn’t important or even because it’s easy to talk about it.

My problem is that we are talking about a very easy form of gratitude, one that isn’t worth very much.

Several years ago, someone sent me a gratitude journal. It was a very nice gesture—I was grateful—but I ended up finding that the whole experience was pretty trite. I would fill the pages with gratitude about my family, my health, my career, the people and things and opportunities in my life that mean a lot to me. But instead of making me feel better, it came to feel sort of pointless and rather repetitive. I was just going through the motions. I wasn’t doing any work.

Tomorrow, which is Thanksgiving in America, is a day we’re supposed to be thankful for many of those same things. Family. Friends. Health. A successful year. A roof over our heads. The food in front of us.

It’s great to be grateful for those things. But that’s sort of my point. You’re grateful because those things are great.

You know the expression that it’s not a principle unless it costs you something? I think it’s true of most good things in life. They ask something of us. You have to work for them.

Courage asks us to face something. Forgiveness asks us to let go of something. Patience asks us to put up with something. Generosity asks us to give up something.

If you’re not working for the gratitude, if it’s not costing you anything, what does it mean?

Marcus Aurelius talks in Meditations about a period of his life where he felt like there was not much to be grateful for. And indeed, it certainly looked like the gods were out to get him. There was the Antonine plague, which would kill literally millions of people during his reign. There were wars, floods, and famines. He would bury several of his children. He was betrayed by his most trusted general in what amounted to an attempted coup. He had health problems. He was away a lot. He did not meet with “the good fortune he deserved,” one ancient historian noted, “as his whole reign was a series of troubles.”

“Convince yourself that everything is the gift of the gods,” he writes in another passage, “that things are good and always will be.”

Think about how hard that must have been, how much convincing that would have taken.

With that in mind, I switched my journaling practice up. What I began to do was try to find ways to express gratitude, not for the things that are easy to be grateful for, but for what is hard:

I am grateful for the insane traffic driving my kids to school—a drive that used to take 35 minutes now regularly taking double that–it gives me more one-on-one time with them.

I am grateful for the people who attack me online—that’s part of having an audience. I get to write for a living. People read what I put out into the world. Of course some of them won’t like or agree with me. They’re keeping me tight. They’re challenging me and making me better.

I am grateful for the uncertainty AI has brought, the disruption it’s causing—it’s forced me to get more creative, to reevaluate where I put my time and energy, and to improve my work…and to learn how to use a new tool (and value the old-school methods more).

I am grateful for the person in town who ripped us off, thinking we wouldn’t notice—they reminded me I can’t be sloppy or take things for granted. They reminded me how much I appreciate all the good, honest people in our lives.

I’m grateful for the argument we had yesterday. I’m grateful for rolling my ankle. I’m grateful for how tired I am. Why? I’m not sure but I’m trying to find a way to be.

I’m grateful for the problems in the world—it’s an opportunity. It gives me, it gives us, the chance to do good (by the way, for the seventh year in a row, we’re raising money for Feeding America through Daily Stoic to donate FOUR MILLION meals to families experiencing hunger. If you have something to spare, I’d love for you to join us at feedingamerica.org/dailystoic).

And on and on.

Do I suddenly enjoy the traffic? Am I now happy that someone tried to steal from me? Am I thrilled to have to rethink and rework parts of how I make a living? Of course not. But in writing these things down, I’m forcing myself to think about them, to reconsider them, and in time, to see some good in them. What they taught me. What they might have spared me from later. What they helped me to stop taking for granted. What they challenged me to get better at.

So, as you gather with family and friends this Thanksgiving, appreciate the obvious gifts—the food, the health, the love in the room. But give some thought to the less obvious gifts too. See if you can find something to be thankful for in the frustrations, the setbacks, the hard times, the people who let you down. Consider how they tested you, stretched you, humbled you. Whatever it is—however difficult, however painful—think about what you might have learned. Think about what you might have gained. Think about how it might have helped make you into who you are.

This is a harder form of gratitude.

One that asks you to think a little harder, look a little longer, dig a little deeper.

This takes time. Effort. Patience. Work.

As most good things in life do.

As I mentioned earlier, we are once again teaming up with Feeding America to help hungry and struggling families.

We donated the first $40,000 and I’d love your help in getting to our goal of $400,000—which would provide over 4 MILLION meals for families across the country! Head over to feedingamerica.org/dailystoic to donate now.

$1 provides 10 meals. Together, we can make a small but meaningful difference in the lives of our neighbors facing hunger.
